name: 名前のないラーメン屋 (Namae no Nai Ramen-ya)

claims.text: Standard ramen/tsukemen shop with wheat noodles and a shared kitchen; no gluten-free handling, dedicated equipment, or separate prep is advertised anywhere.
The signature broths are described as soy-based; Japanese soy sauce used in ramen tare almost always contains wheat, so the tare should be assumed to contain gluten.
Broths are animal-based (seafood/niboshi, chicken, pork) and proteins are offal, chashu pork, and wagyu beef; there is no vegan option and animal products are pervasive in the kitchen.

name: にぼ魂ラーメン 祇園本店 (Nibodamashii Ramen Gion Honten)

claims.text: A wheat-noodle ramen shop with fried side dishes prepared in a tiny shared kitchen; no gluten-free handling or separation is indicated, so cross-contact with wheat is effectively certain.
The tare is a Japanese ramen seasoning, which is overwhelmingly a wheat-containing shoyu base; no wheat-free soy sauce is advertised.
All bowls are built on a dried-sardine fish broth with pork chashu and egg; there is no plant-based broth or vegan preparation, so no item can be considered free of animal cross-contact.

name: Nippon Ramen 凛 KYOTO (Nippon Ramen Rin Kyoto)

claims.text: Bowls are served on house-made wheat noodles (wheat blends such as Haruyokoi and Kitahonami), so wheat is central to the kitchen and there is no gluten-free preparation.
The signature tare is a soy-sauce (shoyu) base; Japanese shoyu is brewed from wheat, so the broth itself contains gluten.
Broths are chicken-based (clear chicken shoyu/shio and a chicken-paitan), with pork chashu and wonton among the toppings; the kitchen is built around animal products with no vegan option.

name: 濃厚京鶏白湯らーめん めんや 美鶴 (Nōkō Kyō Tori Paitan Rāmen Menya Mitsuru)

claims.text: The soy-tare 'black' version of the paitan soba is seasoned with shoyu, which is wheat-containing soy sauce.
All bowls are built on a chicken broth with chicken chashu and chicken tsukune toppings; the shared broth and kitchen make any plant-only request unworkable.

name: 濃厚豚骨ラーメン 岩本家 (Nōkō Tonkotsu Ramen Iwamotoya)

claims.text: Core menu is wheat ramen noodles in a shared pot, with a wheat-based shoyu tare and animal broth; no gluten-free preparation or separation is described.
An iekei tonkotsu-shoyu shop whose tare is soy-sauce based; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat, and no wheat-free tare is offered.
Broth is pork-bone and chicken based and bowls are topped with chashu pork; no vegan or vegetarian option exists, so meat-free dining is not viable.
No allergen information or accommodation is noted in available reviews or shop information.

name: Oike Café × HACHINOBO（オイケカフェ ハチノボウ） (Oike Cafe x Hachinobo)

claims.text: The signature bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles cooked in shared water, with a soy-sauce tare that contains wheat, so cross-contact with gluten is inherent to the kitchen.
The broth is finished with a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare over pork-bone stock; standard Japanese shoyu is brewed with wheat.
Bowls center on pork-bone broth and pork/chicken chashu; any vegetable-leaning dish shares a kitchen that is fundamentally pork-based, so vegan separation is not assured.
Wheat ramen noodles, wheat-flour gyoza skins and soy-based seasonings dominate the menu, cooked on shared woks and surfaces in a small kitchen — high cross-contact risk for gluten throughout.
Dishes are seasoned with Chinese-style soy/oyster sauces (the 御旅丼 sauce is described as a Chinese sauce/oyster-sauce base); standard Japanese and Chinese soy sauces contain wheat.

Cooking centers on pork, egg and seafood across stir-fries, fried rice and gyoza; broths and sauces are meat/seafood based, so any vegetable dish would share equipment and seasonings with animal ingredients.

name: らぁ麺 とうひち (Ra-men Touhichi)

claims.text: The signature bowls are seasoned with raw-pressed (nama-age) soy sauce, which is normally wheat-based; combined with wheat ramen noodles this makes the dishes unsuitable for gluten-free diners.
All broths are chicken-based (tori-seitan clear soup or tori-paitan) and bowls are topped with pork chashu, so the kitchen works with animal products throughout; no vegan preparation is offered.
